title: Trump administration tries to weaken migrant children's legal defense
description_short: Trump administration tries to weaken migrant children's legal defense
description_medium: After the administration failed to eliminate legal funding for unaccompanied minors, it proposed a no-bid award of up to $150 million to Burke Law Group, a Houston firm with 24 lawyers, to represent detained children. The New Yorker reported that the firm lacked the immigration expertise and capacity of established providers, raising questions about whether children would receive meaningful counsel.
description_long: The dispute concerned a federal program that provides legal help to unaccompanied children in immigration custody. The New Yorker reported that the administration had sought to end funding for lawyers representing these minors, then moved to direct as much as $150 million over a year to Burke Law Group in Houston through a single-source agreement. The firm had 24 lawyers, and established providers questioned whether it had sufficient immigration expertise and capacity to handle cases nationwide. Under a 2008 law, unaccompanied children are generally supposed to have access to counsel because of their vulnerability and difficulty navigating immigration proceedings alone. Earlier legal-service providers also said the administration had withheld millions in unpaid fees. The arrangement therefore raised questions about continuity, conflicts, and whether a new contractor could meet the program’s needs. The contract announcement reflected an intent to award, not proof that the firm ultimately received the full amount or that every child lost representation. The concern is attributed to reporting and legal-service advocates, not a court finding that the administration’s purpose was to weaken defense.

preserved_fields.title: Trump administration tries to weaken migrant children's legal defense
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump administration tries to weaken migrant children's legal defense

notes: The New Yorker reports the planned single-source award of up to $150 million, the firm’s size, the 2008 counsel framework, and concerns about expertise and capacity; the notice was an intent to award.

title: Trump's Grab for Power Will Create Secrecy for Him and His Cronies
description_short: Trump's Grab for Power Will Create Secrecy for Him and His Cronies
description_medium: In an August 2026 opinion column, Harvard law professor Noah Feldman criticized Trump’s claim that executive privilege protects presidential conversations with private advisers outside government. Feldman called the position politically unprecedented and legally wrong, warning that it could shield advice from public scrutiny. The article presents a legal argument and forecast, not a court ruling.
description_long: The argument concerned how far executive privilege can extend beyond communications between a president and government officials. In his Sydney Morning Herald column, Harvard law professor Noah Feldman said Trump’s administration was asserting that the privilege could cover presidential conversations with private advisers who do not work for the government. Feldman described that position as unprecedented and legally wrong, and argued that it could create secrecy for people close to the president. Executive privilege is generally invoked to protect confidentiality in presidential decision-making, but courts have treated its scope as limited and subject to competing needs for evidence. The article is commentary by a legal scholar, not a judicial decision resolving the specific claim. It raises a prospective concern: if private conversations are covered broadly, records about advice and influence could be harder to obtain. The description should therefore attribute the legal assessment to Feldman and avoid presenting the predicted secrecy as an outcome already established by a court or investigation.

preserved_fields.title: Trump's Grab for Power Will Create Secrecy for Him and His Cronies
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump's Grab for Power Will Create Secrecy for Him and His Cronies

notes: Noah Feldman’s SMH opinion column describes the asserted privilege for communications with private advisers and gives his legal criticism; this is commentary, not a court ruling.

title: State Lawsuit Alleges White House Orchestrated Campaign Against Colorado
description_short: State Lawsuit Alleges White House Orchestrated Campaign Against Colorado
description_medium: A state lawsuit alleges that the White House orchestrated a campaign against Colorado, with attorneys discovering an email that they describe as a 'smoking gun'. This has raised concerns about the potential for Trump to use the power of the presidency to target his enemies and undermine the rule of law. The lawsuit is seen as a significant challenge to Trump's authority and a reminder that the president is not above the law.
description_long: Colorado Attorney General Phil Weiser’s lawsuit accused the Trump administration of coordinating actions to punish the state. During discovery, state attorneys highlighted an email sent at 2:43 a.m. on December 15 by White House official Emily Underwood. CBS Colorado reported that the message asked officials from several departments—including Transportation, Agriculture, Interior, and Energy, as well as the Office of Management and Budget—to join a call later that day. Colorado’s lawyers called the email a “smoking gun” because they argued it showed coordination at the White House. The email was evidence cited by one side in pending litigation; a court had not determined that it proved an orchestrated campaign. The case therefore concerned both the state’s allegations and the administration’s actions across multiple agencies. The reporting supplies a concrete piece of the record behind the lawsuit, while leaving the legal claims and meaning of the email for the court to assess. The existing description’s broad conclusions should remain attributed to the state’s claims rather than treated as established findings.

preserved_fields.title: State Lawsuit Alleges White House Orchestrated Campaign Against Colorado
preserved_fields.description_short: State Lawsuit Alleges White House Orchestrated Campaign Against Colorado
preserved_fields.description_medium: A state lawsuit alleges that the White House orchestrated a campaign against Colorado, with attorneys discovering an email that they describe as a 'smoking gun'. This has raised concerns about the potential for Trump to use the power of the presidency to target his enemies and undermine the rule of law. The lawsuit is seen as a significant challenge to Trump's authority and a reminder that the president is not above the law.

notes: CBS Colorado identifies the plaintiff, email sender and time, participating agencies, and the state’s “smoking gun” characterization; those claims were being litigated, not adjudicated.

title: ABC Accuses Trump's FCC of Intimidation
description_short: ABC Accuses Trump's FCC of Intimidation
description_medium: ABC and its parent company Disney sued the FCC, alleging that pressure from the Trump administration pushed the network to change programming, including avoiding political candidates on The View. Reuters reported that the suit challenged an early review of licenses for eight Disney-owned stations. FCC Chair Brendan Carr denied that the agency was restricting speech or retaliating against the network.
description_long: The dispute arose after the FCC began an unusually early review of broadcast licenses for eight Disney-owned local stations. ABC and Disney sued the agency, arguing that the review was being used to punish the network over its coverage and force programming changes. Reuters reported that ABC said it avoided booking some political candidates on The View because it feared retaliation. FCC Chair Brendan Carr rejected the accusation, saying the agency was not infringing on Disney’s speech rights or acting because Trump disliked particular content. The competing accounts matter: ABC described a chilling effect, while the regulator denied that the review was intended to control programming. The lawsuit put the FCC’s licensing authority and the First Amendment protections of broadcasters before a court. The available reporting establishes the allegations, the license review, and the FCC’s response, but not a final judicial finding that the agency intimidated ABC. The record should preserve that distinction while explaining why press-freedom advocates viewed the dispute as significant.

preserved_fields.title: ABC Accuses Trump's FCC of Intimidation
preserved_fields.description_short: ABC Accuses Trump's FCC of Intimidation

notes: Reuters reports ABC/Disney’s lawsuit and programming-change allegation, the eight-station license review, and FCC Chair Brendan Carr’s denial; no court ruling is reported.

title: Moves U.S. Embassy to Jerusalem
description_short: The United States opened its embassy in Jerusalem, formalizing the relocation from Tel Aviv.
description_medium: The United States opened its embassy in Jerusalem on May 14, 2018, moving the mission from Tel Aviv and implementing Trump’s December 2017 recognition of Jerusalem as Israel’s capital. The State Department described the opening as fulfilling a promise while reaffirming a commitment to Israeli-Palestinian peace. The decision marked a major change in U.S. diplomatic policy.
description_long: The embassy opened in Jerusalem on May 14, 2018, following Trump’s December 2017 decision to recognize the city as Israel’s capital. The administration initially housed the embassy in an existing U.S. consular building while planning a permanent facility. Secretary of State Mike Pompeo said the opening fulfilled a presidential promise and maintained that the United States remained committed to a comprehensive peace between Israelis and Palestinians. The move reversed decades of U.S. practice of keeping the embassy in Tel Aviv while the city’s status remained disputed. Supporters described the relocation as recognition of Israel’s capital; Palestinian leaders and other critics warned that it prejudged negotiations over Jerusalem. The opening did not resolve the city’s contested status or settle the broader conflict. It was a concrete diplomatic act with symbolic and practical effects: the U.S. mission began operating from Jerusalem, and the decision reshaped how the United States was perceived as a mediator. The record concerns the embassy move itself, while the peace process remained unresolved.

preserved_fields.title: Moves U.S. Embassy to Jerusalem
preserved_fields.description_short: The United States opened its embassy in Jerusalem, formalizing the relocation from Tel Aviv.

notes: The State Department’s May 14, 2018 statement says the opening implemented Trump’s recognition decision and reiterates a peace commitment; PolitiFact records the move from Tel Aviv.

title: Fires FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe
description_short: Trump fired FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe shortly before his retirement amid the Russia probe.
description_medium: Attorney General Jeff Sessions fired FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe on March 16, 2018, about 26 hours before his planned retirement. Sessions cited findings that McCabe had authorized an improper media disclosure and lacked candor with investigators. McCabe disputed the basis for the firing and said Trump’s public criticism made it appear politically motivated.
description_long: McCabe’s firing came just before he planned to retire after more than two decades at the FBI. Attorney General Jeff Sessions dismissed him on March 16, 2018, citing recommendations from the Justice Department inspector general and the FBI’s professional-responsibility office. Those reviews said McCabe had authorized a media disclosure about a Clinton Foundation investigation and had not been candid with investigators about it. McCabe disputed the findings and argued that Trump’s repeated public attacks on him, amid the Russia investigation, raised questions about political influence. Later-released FBI documents added detail about the internal process, but they did not erase the disagreement over motive. The timing affected McCabe’s eligibility for full retirement benefits and made the firing a public controversy. This account distinguishes the stated disciplinary basis from McCabe’s claim of political retaliation; the source material does not establish that Trump personally ordered Sessions to fire him. The event occurred while the FBI and Justice Department were under pressure over politically sensitive investigations.

preserved_fields.title: Fires FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe
preserved_fields.description_short: Trump fired FBI Deputy Director Andrew McCabe shortly before his retirement amid the Russia probe.

notes: NBC News reports McCabe’s March 16 firing shortly before retirement; CREW summarizes the IG/FBI disciplinary findings and McCabe’s dispute over political motivation.
